item.title: How U.S.-Canada Tariff Negotiations Turned Into an All-Out Trade War
item.description: Detailed accounts of the final hours of the negotiations show that, while the United States offered Canada what it said was the best deal of any country, what Canada had to give up in exchange was seen as unthinkable.
item.dc:creator: Matina Stevis-Gridneff and Ana Swanson
item.category: Office of the United States Trade Representative
item.media:description: Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada speaking about the trade dispute with the United States on Monday at the Davie Shipyard in Levis, Quebec.

item.title: What We Know About Australia’s Bird Flu, Which Has Crossed Over to Mammals
item.description: Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 in June in migratory seabirds. Since then, the virus has spread rapidly, straining government responses.
item.dc:creator: Laura Chung
item.media:credit: Joel Carrett/Australian Associated Press, via Reuters
item.media:description: A penguin getting vaccinated on Philip Island, Australia, on Sunday.

item.title: Chinese Artist Sentenced to Three Years in Prison for Mao Sculptures
item.description: Gao Zhen, part of a brotherly duo famous for satirical artworks, was convicted of slandering one of China’s heroes after a secret one-day trial.
item.dc:creator: Lily Kuo
item.media:credit: Shiho Fukada for The New York Times
item.media:description: Gao Zhen, left, and Gao Qiang, with their artwork, “Mao’s Guilt,” in Beijing in 2009.

item.title: A Drone Killed Three Ukrainians. It Was Guided Entirely by A.I.
item.description: An attack by what Ukrainian officials said was a Russian drone with an Nvidia chip presages a dystopian future of weaponry untethered to humans.
item.dc:creator: Andrew E. Kramer and Nicole Tung
item.media:credit: Nicole Tung for The New York Times

item.title: Iran Cracks Down on One Luxury Left to Its Youth: Coffee Shops
item.description: In recent weeks, the police have closed dozens of cafes, often citing laws that stipulate women must veil in public. Experts say the closures are part of an effort to control public space.
item.dc:creator: Leily Nikounazar and Yeganeh Torbati
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:credit: Arash Khamooshi/Polaris for The New York Times
item.media:description: Iranians at a cafe in Tehran in April.

item.title: Can ‘Argentina’s Texas’ Save the Country’s Economy?
item.description: Thousands of Argentines are flocking to a remote stretch of Patagonia, seeking work with only backpacks, tents and the hope that they and their country can turn around their fortunes.
item.dc:creator: Emma Bubola and Sarah Pabst

item.title: As El Niño Dries Indonesia, Wildfires Intensify
item.description: The unusual weather pattern and dried out peatlands, a kind of wetland, have been behind some of the country’s worst fire seasons. This year could be one.
item.dc:creator: Max Kim and Muktita Suhartono
item.media:description: A firefighter battles a wildfire in Ogan Ilir, South Sumatra, Indonesia, earlier this month. This fire season, the country has had an unusually high number of hot spots, according to one estimate.

item.title: UK Prime Minister Burnham Arrives in Ukraine as Russia Amps Up Warnings
item.description: In his first foreign trip since taking office, the British prime minister pledged to stand by Kyiv despite new warnings of potential consequences.
item.dc:creator: Michael D. Shear, Adam Goldman and Jeanna Smialek
item.media:description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain on Monday at the tomb of the unknown soldier at Ukraine’s national military memorial cemetery in Hatne, southwest of Kyiv.

item.title: Iran Pledges to Defy Trump’s Economic Sanctions
item.description: Analysts say Tehran could intensify the dispute militarily after the United States announced new efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. One Iranian official vowed that “not a single drop of oil” would leave the gulf.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Boxerman, Sanam Mahoozi and Ephrat Livni
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:description: Motorists drive past an anti-American billboard in Tehran on Monday. President Trump has threatened Iran with “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

item.title: Syria and Israel Hold U.S.-Mediated Talks to Try to Ease Tensions
item.description: The discussions, reported by the Syrian state news agency, came days after Israel struck an air base in Syria’s northwest, the latest in a series of military interventions.
item.dc:creator: Christina Goldbaum
item.category: Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS)
item.media:description: The Abu al-Duhur air base in northwestern Syria last week after Israeli strikes.

item.title: Some of Russia’s A.I. Drones Are Powered by Nvidia Microcomputers, Ukrainian Officials Say
item.description: The tech giant says it does not sell the devices in Russia, but they are widely available on resale markets. When purchased that way, they are virtually impossible to track.
item.dc:creator: Andrew E. Kramer
item.media:credit: Nicole Tung for The New York Times
item.media:description: A Nvidia Jetson Orin minicomputer that Ukrainian officials say was found in an autonomous drone that Russia recently tested in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine.

item.title: Man Who Told of a Childhood With Wolves Dies at 80

item.dc:creator: Ephrat Livni
item.media:description: Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, right, in Madrid in 2010 at the premiere of “Among Wolves,” a film based on his life, with Juan José Ballesta, left, and Manuel Camacho, the actors who played him as an adult and child.

item.title: A Chinese Robot Beat Usain Bolt’s 100-Meter Record. Should We Be Impressed?
item.description: China’s humanoid robots are achieving superhuman feats of athleticism. But how that translates into the real world is still an open question, experts said.
item.dc:creator: Yan Zhuang

item.title: U.S. Marines Cancel Drill With South Korea, Citing Iran War Demands

United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:description: South Korean marines participate in the Ssangyong, or “Twin Dragons,” exercise in Pohang, South Korea, in 2024.

item.title: U.S. Tariffs Could Price Canadian Firms Out of U.S. and Threaten Thousands of Jobs
item.description: The 50 percent tariffs President Trump imposed on Canadian exports to the United States will make it impossible for many Canadian companies to continue to sell to the U.S. market, economists say.
item.dc:creator: Ian Austen
item.media:description: Harvested logs in British Columbia in 2023. Canada’s forestry industry may be hit particularly hard by the latest American tariffs.

item.title: Iceland’s Murder Rate Is Off the Charts (in Its Books, at Least)
item.description: The Nordic nation has almost no homicides, yet crime fiction is its favorite literary genre. That means writers face a challenge: making murder feel believable.
item.dc:creator: Amelia Nierenberg
item.media:credit: Sigga Ella for The New York Times
item.media:description: Crime novels on display in a bookstore in Reykjavik, Iceland.

item.title: How Argentina’s Oil Boom Is Changing Patagonia
item.description: Our correspondent Emma Bubola travels to northwest Patagonia, the epicenter of an oil boom that Argentina hopes will revolutionize its economy.

item.title: U.S.-Canada Trade War: What to Know About Tariffs and the Negotiations

item.title: Echoing Trump, Latin America’s Leaders Boost Allies Across Borders
item.description: With cheers, endorsements and insults for rivals and “wokismo,” a new crop of right-wing leaders are openly stepping into one another’s elections.

item.media:description: President Javier Milei of Argentina, left, with Flávio Bolsonaro, who hopes to be Brazil’s next president, last month. Mr. Milei’s strident support of Mr. Bolsonaro’s candidacy led to a rift with the current Brazilian president.

item.title: The World’s Breadbaskets Are Getting Pounded by War, Weather and Trade Spats

item.title: Carney Stands Up to Trump in U.S.-Canada Trade War
item.description: Canada’s prime minister walked away from what he thought was a bad trade deal with the United States. Many Canadians are behind him, but it will be costly.

item.title: Lebanon’s Efforts to Tame Hezbollah Stall Amid Israel War

item.title: Yvette Roudy, France’s First Minister for Women’s Rights, Dies at 97
item.description: Maintaining that access to abortion was as much a matter of economic equality as women’s rights, she successfully championed state reimbursement for abortions.
item.dc:creator: Adam Nossiter
item.media:description: Yvette Roudy in 2006. After her death, President Emmanuel Macron of France saluted her for “a life spent making equality between men and women a real right” and for her “untiring capacity for indignation.”

item.title: How Two British Historians Made a Smash Hit Podcast

item.media:description: Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland last month at Hampton Court Palace in southwest London. The podcast they began during the pandemic now gets about 30 million downloads and streams a month.

item.title: How Apartheid Continues to Divide Cape Town

item.title: How a Trump Envoy Uses Vodka and Dirty Jokes to Conduct U.S. Diplomacy

item.title: Sun Screen

item.title: Cities Compete in Dizzying ‘Gold Rush’ to Be Japan’s Backup Capital

item.title: Close and Loving, or Oppressive? A Novelist Takes Aim at Italian Families.

item.media:description: Andrea Bajani in Rome last year. An English translation of his best-selling novel, “The Anniversary,” will be published on Tuesday.

item.title: Canada-U.S. Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse
item.description: Intense negotiations to stave off new levies by the Trump administration ended in an impasse as Mark Carney suspended talks. U.S. tariffs on Canada, and retaliatory tariffs on the U.S., will come into effect.

item.media:description: Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said he suspended the trade talks because the American side introduced last-minute terms that ”called into question the reliability of any deal.”

item.title: Mexican Governor, Accused by U.S. of Helping Cartel, Returns to His Job
item.description: After U.S. prosecutors accused Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya of protecting the Sinaloa cartel, he said he would step down to focus on his defense. On Friday, he declared he was back and faced much criticism.
item.dc:creator: James Wagner
item.media:description: Rubén Rocha Moya, the governor of Sinaloa state, during an annual earthquake drill in Culiacán, Mexico, in 2024.

item.title: Turkey Requests Netanyahu’s Arrest, Saying Israel Abused Flotilla Activists

item.title: Zambia’s Democratic Facade Fractures in Post-Election Crackdown

item.title: Swiss Tourist Sentenced to Prison After Violating ‘Day of Silence’ in Bali

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg Buys an Irish Castle

item.title: Canada-U.S. Tariff Talks Continue as Trump’s Midnight Deadline Looms
